question: I want to do issue 42 myself. How do I stop the bot picking it up in the meantime, and how do I give it back to the bot later?
answer:
To reserve issue #42 for yourself, assign it to yourself with:

```bash
gh issue edit 42 -R Poetic-Poems/<repo> --add-assignee @me
```

Assignment is the reservation switch: `scripts/gather-issues.sh` drops any issue that has an assignee before the Co-Ordinator ever sees the candidate list, so it's never ranked or picked up — the issue stays open and still shows in the dashboard, it's just not selectable. Don't use `Priority: Low` for this (that only affects when it'd be reached, not whether) and don't use the `blocked` label either (that's for work genuinely blocked on something external, not something you've simply claimed).

When you're ready to hand it back to the bot, remove your assignment:

```bash
gh issue edit 42 -R Poetic-Poems/<repo> --remove-assignee @me
```

The very next cycle will have it back in the pool.

question: I asked for changes on one of the bot's pull requests. What will it do with my review, and what do I need to do to get the pull request merged after that?
answer:
I found the full picture.

When you request changes on one of the bot's pull requests, the implementation pipeline (via the `review-feedback` source, `scripts/gather-review-feedback.sh`) will eventually pick that PR up as a candidate — because it's open, carries the pipeline's PR label/branch prefix, and its `reviewDecision` is `CHANGES_REQUESTED`. The Implementer stage then addresses every point from your review (and any inline comments in the same round), pushes a fix commit to the existing branch, and posts one PR comment summarising what it changed for each point (and what it didn't change, and why, if it disagrees with something). It then calls `gh api ... requested_reviewers` to formally re-request your review, since that's the only thing that puts the PR back in your review queue. It leaves the PR ready (not draft).

Crucially, it cannot clear your "Changes requested" status itself: GitHub doesn't let a PR's author approve or dismiss a review on their own PR, and the bot opens PRs under its own account. So the `CHANGES_REQUESTED` decision stays set on the PR even after the fix lands — by design, as the final landing gate. To get it merged, **you need to re-review the PR and submit an approving review** (or otherwise clear the changes-requested state); only then can the pipeline proceed to approve/merge it (it performs the final approval and landing step itself where its trust level allows, but only once a human review is no longer blocking it).

question: The bot closed one of my issues saying the work was already done, but it isn't. I reopened the issue and nothing happened. How do I get the bot to take it on again?
answer:
I found the answer: a plain reopen of a closed issue doesn't bring it back once the pipeline has marked it **void** (its evidence for closing was "it's already done") — only a human can clear a void, and simply reopening the issue isn't the mechanism that does it, by design (so an agent can't make a void item rediscoverable).

To get the bot to take the issue on again, apply the **`unvoided`** label to any issue or pull request that names the item, in that item's repo:

```bash
gh issue edit <n> -R <owner>/<repo> --add-label unvoided
```

The next pipeline cycle reads that label, works out which item(s) it names (from the issue's own number, or a PR's branch/title/body), and reopens any of them that are void — putting the item straight back into the Co-Ordinator's pool that same cycle. Leave the label in place afterward; it's self-limiting (only clears voids recorded *before* it was applied) so it never needs removing. If you'd rather act by hand on a node without waiting for a cycle, you can append an `unvoided` event directly to `~/.local/state/poetic-agents/log.jsonl` as shown in the same section — but note if the work genuinely isn't there, the Implementer may simply void it again, this time with evidence.

question: The bot left one of its own draft pull requests half-finished. Will it come back and finish it, and what should I do if I don't want that draft at all?
answer:
I have what I need to answer.

Yes — the pipeline will come back on its own. Every repository's `sources` list is required to include `abandoned-drafts` (`docs/IMPLEMENTATION-PIPELINE-SPEC.md` requirement 3e): on a later cycle, `scripts/gather-abandoned-drafts.sh` looks for open draft PRs that carry the pipeline's `pr_label`, live on a `branch_prefix`-named branch, and whose *last real activity* (latest of head-commit date, review submissions, or comments — not GitHub's raw `updatedAt`) is older than `abandoned_draft_after_hours`. Once it's that stale, finishing the draft becomes selectable work again, and the pipeline resumes from the existing branch rather than starting over. By default that threshold isn't a fixed number of hours — it's derived to be about "4 cadence firings" of your configured cycle schedule (`abandoned_draft_after_hours` in `config.schema.json`), so with the stock hourly cadence it's on the order of a few hours before it's eligible for pickup.

If you don't want that draft at all, don't close it yourself and expect that to be the end of it — apply the `obsolete` label to the pull request. That label is reserved as a human-only corroboration signal (no pipeline stage may ever apply it; `scripts/doctor.sh` rejects any config that tries to repurpose that name for a configurable label). Once a human has marked the draft `obsolete`, the next cycle's void-closing step (requirement 34k) will corroborate the abandoned-draft void against that label and actually close the pull request for you. Without the label, an open draft that still carries a real diff against its base is instead escalated to a human rather than closed outright, so the label is the deliberate, auditable way to say "this one isn't wanted."

question: My node fires every quarter of an hour, but all morning its log shows each run giving up without doing anything. How do I see why, and is something broken?
answer:
Nothing is broken — this is expected behaviour. The pipeline fires every 15 minutes (`schedule.cycle_interval_minutes`, default 15), but running the Co-Ordinator costs about 2½ minutes of model time every time regardless of whether there's anything to do. So before launching it, the cycle script fingerprints everything the Co-Ordinator's verdict depends on (repo head commits, open issues/PRs, workflow conclusions, blocked/void lists, selection config, prompt hashes); if that fingerprint matches the one recorded against the last "nothing to do" (`none-selected`) verdict, the cycle stands itself down without calling the model at all — a no-op tick. A quiet morning with no repo activity produces exactly this: run after run standing down for the cost of a few `gh` calls.

To see this isn't a malfunction, check the dashboard or the log directly:

- `tail -f ~/.local/state/poetic-agents/<...>-log.jsonl` (the node's own event stream) — each no-op tick logs the stand-down/skip, rather than silently doing nothing.
- The local dashboard's `noop_ticks` summary (shown beneath the recent-cycles table) totals these no-op ticks, split by `standdown` vs `skipped` (lock held) vs `overlap`, instead of giving each one its own row.

It will only run for real once something in that fingerprint changes (a commit, a new issue, a changed PR, etc.), or after `none_selected_recheck_hours` forces a re-check regardless — so if it truly never runs real work again past that window, that's the actual signal to investigate, not the quiet mornings themselves.

question: What am I going to be paying for in model usage? Which part is the expensive part, and does it still cost money when there is nothing to do?
answer:
I have what I need to answer clearly.

You're paying for model API usage at several distinct stages, each configured with its own model in `config.json` (README.md's "Configuration" table, lines 506–518):

- **Co-Ordinator** (`coordinator_model`, default `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`) — cheap triage, picks what to work on next.
- **Implementer** (`implementer_model_default`/`_trivial`) — does the actual code changes; Sonnet for real code, Haiku for trivial docs/comments.
- **Reviewer** (`reviewer_model_default`/`_complex`) — quality gate before landing; Sonnet normally, Opus for work graded `complexity:high`.
- **Approver** (`approver_model_default`/`_complex`/`_critical`) — the merge-approval gate, escalating to Opus or even `claude-fable-5` for the rarest, most contested cases.
- **Enabler** (`enabler_model`, default `claude-opus-5`) — re-examines long-blocked items; the README explicitly flags this as "the most expensive model here", though it's engaged rarely.

So the single most expensive *tier* is the Enabler/Approver-critical path (Opus/Fable-class models), but they fire infrequently. The stage that actually dominates spend day-to-day is the **Co-Ordinator**, because it fires on every scheduled cycle (every 15 minutes by default) — and per "Skipping no-op cycles" (README.md:1471), it costs the same whether it finds work or not: "about 2½ minutes of Haiku" per call, every time it runs.

To your last question — yes, **it does cost money even when there's nothing to do, unless the no-op short-circuit catches it**. The Script fingerprints everything the Co-Ordinator's verdict depends on (head commits, issues, PRs, workflow results, etc.) before launching it; if nothing has changed since the last "nothing to do" verdict, the cycle stands down for the price of a few free `gh` API calls instead of paying for a Co-Ordinator invocation. Without that check, a quiet week would mean a paid Haiku call roughly every 15 minutes just to hear "nothing changed" again. The `none_selected_recheck_hours` setting also forces a real (paid) Co-Ordinator run at least once a day regardless, as a safety net.

question: If I run it on two machines for redundancy, what stops both of them picking up the same issue and doing the work twice?
answer:
I have enough now to answer concisely.

The pipeline is explicitly built to run on several machines at once, and the mechanism that stops two of them from doing the same issue twice is the atomic per-item **claim** taken by the Script itself (never the model) before any work starts — requirement 17a in `docs/IMPLEMENTATION-PIPELINE-SPEC.md`.

For a fresh item, this is a "branch claim": the Script tries to create the branch `agent/<item-ref>` on the target repo via a create-only `POST /git/refs`. Because the ref name is derived deterministically from the item, every node computes the identical branch name for the same item, and GitHub's own atomicity arbitrates the race — a 422 means a peer already won, so that node logs `claim-lost` and falls through to the next candidate in its ranked list (bounded by `candidates_max`, default 3). For finishing-source work (review feedback, merge-conflicts, dequeued, abandoned-drafts), it's a "file claim" instead: a create-only PUT of `claims/<repo>/<ref>.json` in the state repository, so two nodes racing to finish/rebase/fix the same PR contend on the same file and only one wins. There's additionally a PR-keyed claim (`pr-<n>`) taken right after the item claim, closing a gap where two different rounds/heads of the *same* PR could otherwise be claimed separately by different nodes (issue #238).

A stale claim left by a dead node is garbage-collected after `claim_ttl_hours` (every node runs `lib/claim.sh gc`), so a crashed machine doesn't permanently block the item. In short: it's safe to run on two (or more) machines because the Script's atomic claim primitive, not any coordination between the machines, is what makes a double-pickup impossible.

question: If I let it merge on its own and it starts doing something I do not like, how do I keep a veto over a single pull request, and how do I stop the automatic merging, or everything, at once?

question: shellcheck is clean on my laptop, but the shell-lint check fails on my pull request. What is CI doing differently, and how do I reproduce it before pushing?
answer:
Two things most likely differ:

1. **Pinned shellcheck version.** CI installs exactly `v0.10.0` (checksum-verified) — `.github/workflows/shellcheck.yml`'s `SHELLCHECK_VERSION`/`SHELLCHECK_SHA256`. If your laptop has a newer/older shellcheck, it can report (or fail to report) findings the pinned version doesn't.

2. **The size guard in `scripts/lint-shell.sh`.** Normally the script estimates the memory cost of running `shellcheck -x` (which follows every `# shellcheck source=` target) against the memory actually available on the machine running it, and on a budget-constrained machine it will silently degrade some files — linting them *without* `-x` and suppressing SC1091/SC2154/SC2034 — or skip the biggest ones entirely, printing a warning rather than failing. CI sets `LINT_SHELL_FOLLOW_MIB=0`, which disables that guard outright and forces every file through the full `-x` path regardless of estimated cost, because the runner has the memory and "clean" should mean everything was actually checked. Your laptop, with less reported `MemAvailable`, may have degraded or skipped some files and come back "clean" without ever running the checks CI did.

To reproduce CI's exact check before pushing, run the same invocation CI uses:

```
LINT_SHELL_FOLLOW_MIB=0 ./scripts/lint-shell.sh
```

That forces full `-x` following on every file just as the workflow does, so you'll see the same findings. If you want to be fully sure the version matches too, confirm your local `shellcheck --version` is `0.10.0`.
